entry.title: Robotics foundations: transforms, kinematics, control and planning

link.title: Robotics foundations: transforms, kinematics, control and planning

entry.content:
Why this matters

Embodied AI is the part of AI that has to move a body through the physical world. Modern robot learning papers talk about “policies”, “action chunks” and “end-effector deltas”, but underneath every one of them sits a stack of classical robotics: coordinate frames, kinematics, dynamics, low-level controllers and planners. A Vision-Language-Action model that outputs a 7-D end-effector command is useless unless something converts that command into joint torques at 1 kHz without hitting joint limits or itself.

This first post of the Embodied AI track is a compact tour of that stack, written for readers who know deep learning, graphics and world models but have little robotics background. If you have done graphics you already know half of it: a robot arm is a scene graph of rigid transforms, and inverse kinematics is the same problem that animators solve for character rigs.

Prerequisites

  • Linear algebra: matrices, rotations, least squares, the SVD.
  • Calculus: partial derivatives, the chain rule.
  • Python and NumPy.
  • Helpful but optional: homogeneous coordinates from a graphics course.

1. Rigid-body transforms and SE(3)

Rotations: SO(3)

The orientation of a rigid body relative to a reference frame is a rotation matrix $R \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ whose columns are the body’s axes expressed in the reference frame. Rotation matrices form the special orthogonal group

\[SO(3) = \{ R \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} \;:\; R^\top R = I,\; \det R = 1 \}.\]

SO(3) is a 3-dimensional manifold, not a vector space: you cannot add two rotations and get a rotation. Common parameterizations are Euler angles (minimal but singular at “gimbal lock”), unit quaternions (4 numbers, double cover, no singularities, the standard in simulators and game engines), and the axis-angle / exponential coordinates $\omega\theta$ with unit axis $\hat\omega$ and angle $\theta$.

For a vector $\omega = (\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3)$ define the skew-symmetric matrix

\[[\omega] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega_3 & \omega_2 \\ \omega_3 & 0 & -\omega_1 \\ -\omega_2 & \omega_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\omega]\,v = \omega \times v .\]

The matrix exponential maps axis-angle to a rotation (Rodrigues’ formula):

\[R = e^{[\hat\omega]\theta} = I + \sin\theta\,[\hat\omega] + (1-\cos\theta)\,[\hat\omega]^2 .\]

The set of skew-symmetric matrices is the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, the tangent space of SO(3) at the identity. Angular velocity lives there: if $R(t)$ is a trajectory, then $\dot R R^\top = [\omega_s]$ gives the angular velocity in the fixed (space) frame and $R^\top \dot R = [\omega_b]$ in the body frame.

Rigid motions: SE(3)

A full pose (position $p$ and orientation $R$) is a homogeneous transform

\[T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in SE(3), \qquad T^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} R^\top & -R^\top p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.\]

This is exactly the 4x4 model matrix from graphics. Notation that saves a lot of bugs: write $T_{ab}$ for “the pose of frame $b$ expressed in frame $a$”. Then composition chains like dominoes,

\[T_{ac} = T_{ab}\,T_{bc}, \qquad p_a = T_{ab}\, p_b \;\text{(in homogeneous coordinates)}.\]

The robot’s whole “scene graph” (world, base, links, camera, gripper, object) is a tree of such transforms. Hand-eye calibration, for example, is the problem of estimating the fixed $T_{\text{gripper},\text{camera}}$.

Twists and screws

The velocity of a rigid body is a twist $\mathcal{V} = (\omega, v) \in \mathbb{R}^6$, with $[\mathcal{V}] = \begin{bmatrix}[\omega] & v\0&0\end{bmatrix} \in \mathfrak{se}(3)$. Chasles’ theorem says every rigid motion is a rotation about an axis combined with a translation along it, a screw motion, and the exponential map $T = e^{[\mathcal{S}]\theta}$ turns a unit screw axis $\mathcal{S}$ and a distance $\theta$ into an element of SE(3). This is the foundation of the product-of-exponentials (PoE) formula used throughout Modern Robotics. The dual of a twist is a wrench $\mathcal{F} = (m, f)$ (moment and force); power is $\mathcal{F}^\top\mathcal{V}$.

Why care as a learning person? Because action spaces are poses. Predicting a rotation with a network means choosing a representation: Euler angles have discontinuities, quaternions have the $q \equiv -q$ ambiguity, and Zhou et al. (CVPR 2019) showed that a continuous 6-D representation (two columns of $R$, re-orthonormalized) is easier to regress. Many policies (e.g. Diffusion Policy in post 4) use it.

2. Forward kinematics

A serial manipulator is a chain of links connected by joints, usually revolute (R) or prismatic (P). The configuration is the vector of joint values $q \in \mathbb{R}^n$; the set of all configurations is the configuration space (C-space). Forward kinematics (FK) maps $q$ to the end-effector pose:

\[T_{0n}(q) = T_{01}(q_1)\,T_{12}(q_2)\cdots T_{n-1,n}(q_n).\]

Denavit-Hartenberg parameters

Denavit and Hartenberg (1955) showed that by placing frames cleverly, each link transform needs only four numbers. In the standard DH convention the $z_i$ axis is the axis of joint $i+1$ and

\[T_{i-1,i} = \mathrm{Rot}_z(\theta_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_z(d_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_x(a_i)\,\mathrm{Rot}_x(\alpha_i) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i & -\sin\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & \sin\theta_i\sin\alpha_i & a_i\cos\theta_i\\ \sin\theta_i & \cos\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & -\cos\theta_i\sin\alpha_i & a_i\sin\theta_i\\ 0 & \sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i & d_i\\ 0&0&0&1 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Parameter Meaning
$a_i$ link length: distance between $z_{i-1}$ and $z_i$ along $x_i$
$\alpha_i$ link twist: angle from $z_{i-1}$ to $z_i$ about $x_i$
$d_i$ link offset: distance along $z_{i-1}$ (variable for a prismatic joint)
$\theta_i$ joint angle about $z_{i-1}$ (variable for a revolute joint)

Beware: there is also a modified DH convention (Craig), used e.g. in Franka Emika’s documentation, with a different order of the four elementary transforms. Mixing the two is a classic source of bugs. In practice robots are described with URDF or MJCF files (post 3) that store a full transform per joint, and libraries such as Pinocchio, Drake, MuJoCo or PyBullet compute FK for you. DH is still worth knowing because it makes the structure explicit and is how most textbooks and datasheets present kinematics.

A planar 3-link arm in NumPy

For a planar arm, every $\alpha_i = d_i = 0$, so each DH transform is a rotation by $q_i$ followed by a translation $a_i$ along the new $x$ axis. With absolute angles $c_i = q_1 + \dots + q_i$, the end effector is

\[p_x = \sum_i a_i\cos c_i,\qquad p_y = \sum_i a_i \sin c_i,\qquad \phi = c_n .\] 
import numpy as np

def dh(a, alpha, d, theta):
    """Standard DH transform: Rot_z(theta) Trans_z(d) Trans_x(a) Rot_x(alpha)."""
    ct, st, ca, sa = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta), np.cos(alpha), np.sin(alpha)
    return np.array([[ct, -st * ca,  st * sa, a * ct],
                     [st,  ct * ca, -ct * sa, a * st],
                     [0.0,     sa,       ca,      d],
                     [0.0,    0.0,      0.0,    1.0]])

LINKS = np.array([1.0, 0.8, 0.5])          # link lengths of a planar 3R arm

def fk(q, links=LINKS):
    """Forward kinematics: returns the 4x4 pose of the end effector and all joint positions."""
    T = np.eye(4)
    pts = [T[:3, 3].copy()]
    for a, theta in zip(links, q):
        T = T @ dh(a, 0.0, 0.0, theta)     # planar arm: alpha = d = 0
        pts.append(T[:3, 3].copy())
    return T, np.array(pts)

def task(q):
    """Task-space coordinates x = (px, py, phi) of the end effector."""
    T, _ = fk(q)
    return np.array([T[0, 3], T[1, 3], np.arctan2(T[1, 0], T[0, 0])])

pts gives every joint position, which is all you need to draw the arm with matplotlib.

3. Jacobians and differential kinematics

FK is nonlinear, but its derivative is linear in the joint velocities:

\[\dot x = J(q)\,\dot q, \qquad J(q) = \frac{\partial x}{\partial q} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.\]

For our planar arm ($m = n = 3$) the columns are easy to derive by differentiating the sums above:

\[J_{1i} = -\sum_{k\ge i} a_k \sin c_k,\qquad J_{2i} = \sum_{k\ge i} a_k\cos c_k, \qquad J_{3i} = 1 .\]

For a general spatial arm, the geometric Jacobian column of a revolute joint $i$ with unit axis $z_{i-1}$ through point $o_{i-1}$ (both in the base frame) is

\[J_i = \begin{bmatrix} z_{i-1}\times(o_n - o_{i-1}) \\ z_{i-1}\end{bmatrix},\]

stacking linear velocity over angular velocity; a prismatic joint contributes $(z_{i-1}, 0)$. (Modern Robotics writes the same thing with space and body Jacobians built from screw axes.)

The Jacobian tells you almost everything about local behaviour:

  • Singularities: where $\operatorname{rank} J < m$ the end effector loses a direction of motion (a fully stretched arm cannot move further outward). Near them, small Cartesian motions require huge joint speeds.
  • Manipulability: Yoshikawa’s measure $w = \sqrt{\det(JJ^\top)}$, the volume of the velocity ellipsoid $\lbrace J\dot q : \lVert\dot q\rVert \le 1 \rbrace$, whose axes come from the SVD of $J$.
  • Statics: by the principle of virtual work, a wrench $\mathcal{F}$ at the end effector requires joint torques $\tau = J^\top(q)\,\mathcal{F}$. This one line is the basis of force and impedance control.
  • Redundancy: if $n > m$ (e.g. a 7-DoF arm for a 6-D pose) there is a null space; joint motions $(I - J^+J)\,z$ move the elbow without moving the hand.

Always test a hand-written Jacobian against finite differences:

def jacobian(q, links=LINKS):
    """Analytic Jacobian d(px, py, phi)/dq of the planar arm."""
    c = np.cumsum(q)                        # absolute link angles
    J = np.zeros((3, len(q)))
    for i in range(len(q)):
        J[0, i] = -np.sum(links[i:] * np.sin(c[i:]))
        J[1, i] = np.sum(links[i:] * np.cos(c[i:]))
        J[2, i] = 1.0
    return J

q = np.array([0.3, -0.5, 0.8])
eps = 1e-6
J_num = np.stack([(task(q + eps * np.eye(3)[i]) - task(q - eps * np.eye(3)[i])) / (2 * eps)
                  for i in range(3)], axis=1)
print("Jacobian error:", np.abs(J_num - jacobian(q)).max())   # ~1e-10

4. Inverse kinematics

Inverse kinematics (IK) asks for $q$ such that \(x(q) = x^{\ast}\). It can have zero, finitely many, or infinitely many solutions.

Analytic IK

For simple or specially designed arms there are closed-form solutions. For a planar 2-link arm reaching $(p_x, p_y)$, the law of cosines gives

\[\cos q_2 = \frac{p_x^2 + p_y^2 - a_1^2 - a_2^2}{2a_1a_2},\qquad q_2 = \pm\arccos(\cdot),\qquad q_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(p_y, p_x) - \operatorname{atan2}(a_2\sin q_2,\; a_1 + a_2\cos q_2),\]

with the $\pm$ selecting “elbow up” or “elbow down”, and no solution when $\lvert\cos q_2\rvert > 1$. Industrial 6-DoF arms with a spherical wrist (last three axes intersecting) decouple into a position problem and an orientation problem (Pieper’s criterion) and have up to 8 analytic solutions. Tools such as IKFast (OpenRAVE) generate these solvers automatically.

Numerical IK: Newton, Jacobian transpose, pseudoinverse

For general arms we iterate. Linearize around the current $q$: \(x^{\ast} - x(q) \approx J\,\Delta q\). Options:

  • Jacobian transpose: $\Delta q = \alpha J^\top e$. Cheap, always a descent direction for $\tfrac12\lVert e\rVert^2$, but slow.
  • Pseudoinverse (Gauss-Newton): $\Delta q = J^+ e$ with $J^+ = J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}$ for a wide $J$. Fast near a solution but explodes near singularities because $J^+$ has $1/\sigma_i$ terms.
  • Damped least squares (DLS, Levenberg-Marquardt): minimize $\lVert J\Delta q - e\rVert^2 + \lambda^2\lVert\Delta q\rVert^2$, giving
\[\Delta q = J^\top\left(JJ^\top + \lambda^2 I\right)^{-1} e = \sum_i \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \lambda^2}\, v_i u_i^\top e .\]

The SVD form shows why DLS is robust (Nakamura and Hanafusa 1986; Wampler 1986): directions with $\sigma_i \gg \lambda$ behave like the pseudoinverse, while directions with $\sigma_i \to 0$ are damped to zero instead of blowing up. The price is slower convergence and a small bias.

def wrap(a):
    return (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi

def ik_dls(x_goal, q0, lam=0.05, iters=200, tol=1e-6):
    """Damped least-squares IK: dq = J^T (J J^T + lam^2 I)^-1 e."""
    q = q0.astype(float).copy()
    for k in range(iters):
        e = x_goal - task(q)
        e[2] = wrap(e[2])                   # angle error must be wrapped
        if np.linalg.norm(e) < tol:
            break
        J = jacobian(q)
        dq = J.T @ np.linalg.solve(J @ J.T + lam**2 * np.eye(3), e)
        q += dq
    return q, k, np.linalg.norm(e)

x_goal = np.array([1.2, 0.9, np.pi / 4])
q_sol, n, err = ik_dls(x_goal, np.zeros(3))
print(np.round(q_sol, 4), n, err)           # converges in ~8 iterations, residual ~1e-7
print(np.round(task(q_sol), 4))             # [1.2, 0.9, 0.7854]

# unreachable target (total reach is 2.3): with lam=0.5 the arm stretches toward it,
# residual 0.7 = the best achievable. With lam=0.05 the iteration oscillates near the singularity.
q_far, n, err = ik_dls(np.array([3.0, 0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.1]), lam=0.5, iters=500)
print(err)                                  # 0.7

Try the last call with lam=0.05: the iterate wanders around with a residual of several units, because the stretched-out arm is singular and lightly-damped steps overshoot. Production IK solvers combine DLS with adaptive damping, step-size limits, joint limits and secondary objectives in the null space; the modern formulation is a small quadratic program (QP) per control tick, e.g. “minimize task error subject to joint position and velocity limits”, solved by libraries such as Pink, mink or Drake.

5. A short look at dynamics

Kinematics ignores forces. The equations of motion of an $n$-joint rigid-body system are

\[M(q)\,\ddot q + C(q,\dot q)\,\dot q + g(q) = \tau + J(q)^\top \mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}},\]

with the symmetric positive-definite mass matrix $M(q)$, Coriolis and centrifugal terms $C\dot q$, gravity $g(q)$, joint torques $\tau$ and external wrenches \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}}\) (e.g. contacts). They come from the Euler-Lagrange equations with Lagrangian $L = \tfrac12 \dot q^\top M(q)\dot q - V(q)$. Two standard problems:

  • Inverse dynamics: given $q, \dot q, \ddot q$, compute $\tau$. The recursive Newton-Euler algorithm (RNEA) does this in $O(n)$.
  • Forward dynamics: given $\tau$, compute $\ddot q = M^{-1}(\tau - C\dot q - g)$. The articulated-body algorithm (ABA) is also $O(n)$ (Featherstone 2008).

Two structural facts make control design possible: $M(q)$ is positive definite, and with a suitable choice of $C$ the matrix $\dot M - 2C$ is skew-symmetric (passivity). Contacts, friction and actuator limits make real dynamics much harder; that is the job of the physics engines in post 3.

6. Control

The controller turns a desired trajectory into torques, typically at 0.5 to 1 kHz on the robot, while a learned policy runs at 5 to 50 Hz on top of it. Knowing which layer your policy commands (joint position targets, joint velocities, end-effector poses, torques) matters a lot for sim-to-real.

PID and PD with gravity compensation

The workhorse is PID on each joint:

\[\tau = K_p\, e + K_i \int_0^t e\, dt' - K_d\,\dot q, \qquad e = q_{\text{ref}} - q .\]

The proportional term acts as a spring, the derivative term as a damper, and the integral term removes steady-state error caused by constant disturbances such as gravity. A better use of a model is PD plus gravity compensation, $\tau = K_p e - K_d\dot q + g(q)$, which for a constant target is globally asymptotically stable (Takegaki and Arimoto 1981). A one-joint pendulum makes the difference visible:

import numpy as np

# 1-DoF pendulum joint: I*qdd + b*qd + m*g*l*sin(q) = tau
I, b, m, g, l = 0.5, 0.1, 1.0, 9.81, 0.5
dt, T = 1e-3, 3.0

def simulate(Kp, Kd, Ki, gravity_comp, q_ref=np.pi / 3):
    q, qd, integ = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(int(T / dt)):
        e = q_ref - q
        integ += e * dt
        tau = Kp * e - Kd * qd + Ki * integ
        if gravity_comp:
            tau += m * g * l * np.sin(q)      # feed-forward model term
        qdd = (tau - b * qd - m * g * l * np.sin(q)) / I
        qd += qdd * dt                        # semi-implicit Euler
        q += qd * dt
    return q_ref - q

print("PD only        error %.4f rad" % simulate(20, 3, 0, False))   # 0.1861
print("PID            error %.4f rad" % simulate(20, 3, 30, False))  # 0.0000
print("PD + gravity   error %.4f rad" % simulate(20, 3, 0, True))    # -0.0001

Plain PD sags by about 0.19 rad because the spring must hold up the weight; the integral term or the gravity model removes the error. Legged-robot RL policies (post 2) almost always output joint position targets to such a PD loop instead of raw torques; the PD gains then become part of the “action space”.

Computed torque and operational-space control

If the model is good, cancel the nonlinear dynamics and impose linear error dynamics (computed torque, or feedback linearization):

\[\tau = M(q)\left(\ddot q_{\text{ref}} + K_d\dot e + K_p e\right) + C\dot q + g .\]

Khatib’s operational-space formulation (1987) does the same in task space. With the task-space inertia $\Lambda(q) = (J M^{-1} J^\top)^{-1}$ the end effector behaves like a body of mass $\Lambda$, and

\[\tau = J^\top\left(\Lambda\,\ddot x_{\text{cmd}} + \mu + p\right) + \left(I - J^\top \bar J^{\top}\right)\tau_0, \qquad \bar J = M^{-1}J^\top\Lambda,\]

where $\mu, p$ are the task-space Coriolis and gravity terms and $\tau_0$ is a secondary objective projected into the dynamically consistent null space (e.g. keep the elbow near a rest pose).

Impedance control

Hogan’s impedance control (1985) does not try to track a position stiffly; it makes the end effector behave like a mass-spring-damper around a target:

\[\Lambda_d\,\ddot{\tilde x} + D_d\,\dot{\tilde x} + K_d\,\tilde x = \mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}},\qquad \tilde x = x - x_d .\]

The simplest implementation ignores the desired inertia and commands $\tau = J^\top\left(K_d (x_d - x) - D_d\,\dot x\right) + g(q)$, using the static relation $\tau = J^\top\mathcal{F}$. Low stiffness gives compliant, safe contact (wiping, insertion, human interaction); high stiffness gives accurate tracking. Many learned manipulation policies output a target pose $x_d$ at 10 to 20 Hz to a Cartesian impedance controller running at 1 kHz; some also predict the stiffness (“variable impedance”).

7. Motion planning

Planning finds a collision-free path in C-space from $q_{\text{start}}$ to $q_{\text{goal}}$. Obstacles in the workspace become complicated “C-obstacles” in joint space, so planners query a collision checker (which runs FK and mesh-mesh tests, the same BVH machinery as in ray tracing) instead of building the free space explicitly.

Graph search: A*

On a discretized C-space (grid or lattice), A* (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael 1968) expands nodes in order of $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, cost-so-far plus a heuristic estimate of cost-to-go. If $h$ is admissible (never overestimates) A* returns an optimal path; if it is also consistent (\(h(n) \le c(n,n') + h(n')\)) no node needs to be re-expanded. Dijkstra is A* with $h = 0$. Grids scale exponentially with dimension, so A* is used for mobile robots in 2-D/3-D, footstep planning and discretized lattices, not for 7-DoF arms.

Sampling-based planning: PRM, RRT, RRT*

Sampling-based planners avoid discretization. PRM (Kavraki et al. 1996) samples many collision-free configurations, connects nearby ones and answers queries with graph search. RRT (LaValle 1998) grows a tree from the start: sample $x_{\text{rand}}$, find the nearest tree node, step a fixed distance toward the sample, and add the new node if the edge is collision free. The Voronoi bias of this procedure pulls the tree into unexplored space. RRT is probabilistically complete (it finds a path with probability approaching 1 if one exists) but not optimal. RRT* (Karaman and Frazzoli 2011) adds two steps, choosing the best parent within a shrinking radius $r_n \propto (\log n / n)^{1/d}$ and rewiring neighbours through the new node, which makes it asymptotically optimal.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
OBST = [(np.array([0.5, 0.5]), 0.2), (np.array([0.25, 0.8]), 0.12)]   # circles (center, radius)

def free(p):
    return all(np.linalg.norm(p - c) > r for c, r in OBST)

def edge_free(a, b, n=20):
    return all(free(a + t * (b - a)) for t in np.linspace(0, 1, n))

def rrt(start, goal, step=0.05, iters=5000, goal_bias=0.1):
    nodes, parent = [start], [-1]
    for _ in range(iters):
        x_rand = goal if rng.random() < goal_bias else rng.random(2)   # sample in [0,1]^2
        i = int(np.argmin([np.linalg.norm(n - x_rand) for n in nodes]))
        d = x_rand - nodes[i]
        x_new = nodes[i] + d * min(1.0, step / (np.linalg.norm(d) + 1e-12))  # steer
        if not edge_free(nodes[i], x_new):
            continue
        nodes.append(x_new); parent.append(i)
        if np.linalg.norm(x_new - goal) < step and edge_free(x_new, goal):
            nodes.append(goal); parent.append(len(nodes) - 2)
            path, j = [], len(nodes) - 1
            while j != -1:
                path.append(nodes[j]); j = parent[j]
            return np.array(path[::-1]), len(nodes)
    return None, len(nodes)

path, n = rrt(np.array([0.1, 0.1]), np.array([0.9, 0.9]))
print(f"tree size {n}, path waypoints {len(path)}, "
      f"length {np.sum(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(path, axis=0), axis=1)):.3f}")

To plan for the 3-link arm instead of a point, replace the sample space by $[-\pi,\pi]^3$ and free(q) by “FK the links and test each segment against the obstacles”. RRT paths are jagged, so real systems shortcut and smooth them, then time-parameterize them under velocity and acceleration limits (e.g. TOPP-RA). Trajectory optimization methods such as CHOMP (Ratliff et al. 2009) and TrajOpt (Schulman et al. 2013) instead optimize a whole trajectory for smoothness plus collision cost, and GPU-parallel planners like NVIDIA cuRobo bring planning times to milliseconds.

Where learning enters

Classical block Learned replacement or augmentation (later posts)
Hand-designed controller RL policy that outputs PD targets (post 2)
Analytic model Simulator with domain randomization, or a learned world model (posts 3, 5)
Planner + cost function Policy imitating demonstrations, e.g. ACT, Diffusion Policy (post 4)
Task specification in code Language instruction to a VLA model (post 5)

Learning rarely removes the lower layers: an OpenVLA or pi0 policy still sends targets to an IK solver and an impedance or PD controller. Understanding those layers is how you debug a policy that “works in sim but jitters on the robot”.

Try it

The home page Lab has an XPBD cloth demo. Position-based dynamics solves constraints by projecting positions, much like the IK iterations above project an arm onto the “reach the target” constraint; dragging a cloth particle is literally an IK problem for a very redundant chain. A good exercise is to port ik_dls to JavaScript and drag the end effector of a 3-link arm on a canvas.

Representative papers

Paper Venue Year Link Why it matters
Denavit and Hartenberg, A kinematic notation for lower-pair mechanisms based on matrices J. Applied Mechanics 1955 DOI The DH convention
Hart, Nilsson, Raphael, A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths IEEE Trans. SSC 1968 DOI A* search
Hogan, Impedance control: an approach to manipulation, Part I J. Dyn. Sys., Meas., Control 1985 DOI Impedance control
Nakamura and Hanafusa, Inverse kinematic solutions with singularity robustness for robot manipulator control J. Dyn. Sys., Meas., Control 1986 - Damped least-squares IK
Khatib, A unified approach for motion and force control of robot manipulators: the operational space formulation IEEE J. Robotics and Automation 1987 DOI Operational-space control
Kavraki et al., Probabilistic roadmaps for path planning in high-dimensional configuration spaces IEEE Trans. Robotics and Automation 1996 DOI PRM
LaValle, Rapidly-exploring random trees: a new tool for path planning Tech. report, Iowa State 1998 - RRT
Karaman and Frazzoli, Sampling-based algorithms for optimal motion planning IJRR 2011 arXiv RRT*, PRM*, asymptotic optimality
Schulman et al., Finding locally optimal, collision-free trajectories with sequential convex optimization RSS 2013 PDF TrajOpt
Zhou et al., On the continuity of rotation representations in neural networks CVPR 2019 arXiv The 6-D rotation representation used by many policies

Learning resources

  • K. Lynch and F. Park, Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control (Cambridge University Press, 2017), free PDF, videos and code on the book page. Chapters 3 to 6 and 8 to 11 cover this post in depth with screw theory.
  • R. Tedrake, Robotic Manipulation and Underactuated Robotics, MIT course notes with runnable Drake notebooks.
  • S. LaValle, Planning Algorithms (Cambridge, 2006), free online.
  • R. Featherstone, Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms (Springer, 2008), for RNEA/ABA.
  • B. Siciliano, L. Sciavicco, L. Villani, G. Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control (Springer, 2009).
  • Code: Pinocchio (fast rigid-body dynamics), Drake, OMPL (sampling-based planners), Peter Corke’s Robotics Toolbox for Python.

Exercises

  1. Implement the analytic 2-link IK above and check both elbow solutions with fk.
  2. Write the geometric Jacobian for a 3-D arm given by a DH table and verify it with finite differences. Plot the manipulability $\sqrt{\det JJ^\top}$ of the planar arm over its workspace.
  3. Add joint limits to ik_dls by clamping, then by a null-space term that pushes joints to the middle of their range. Compare how often each version reaches random targets.
  4. Extend the pendulum example to a 2-link arm with $M(q)$ and compare PD, PID and computed torque under a 10% error in the link masses.
  5. Turn rrt into RRT* (choose-parent and rewire) and plot path length versus number of samples.

Next: Reinforcement learning for robots, where controllers stop being designed and start being learned.
entry.summary: SE(3), forward and inverse kinematics, Jacobians, a first look at dynamics, PID and impedance control, and A*/RRT planning, with NumPy code for a 3-link arm.

entry.title: From phone capture to VR: a hands-on 3D Gaussian Splatting tutorial

link.title: From phone capture to VR: a hands-on 3D Gaussian Splatting tutorial

entry.content:
Why this matters

Five posts of theory are worth little until you have captured and explored a scene of your own. This tutorial walks through the whole pipeline on a single consumer GPU: capture → poses (COLMAP) → training (3DGS) → cleanup and export → viewing in the browser and in VR. Each step connects back to the theory: the camera models and SfM of post 1, the optimization of post 4, and the anti-aliasing and VR concerns of post 5. When something goes wrong, and something always does, the failure-mode table at the end tells you which of those ideas to revisit.

Tools change quickly. The commands below were checked against the current sources of COLMAP, the official 3DGS repository, gsplat and nerfstudio; if a flag has been renamed in your version, --help is the source of truth.

Prerequisites

  • An NVIDIA GPU with CUDA (8 GB of VRAM is enough for small scenes at reduced resolution; 24 GB is comfortable for full-resolution outdoor scenes), Linux or Windows.
  • Python 3.10+ with PyTorch and CUDA, conda or venv, ffmpeg, and COLMAP (prebuilt binaries or a CUDA build).
  • A phone or camera. Optional: a WebXR-capable headset (for example a standalone headset with a Chromium-based browser).

1. Capture

Capture quality decides the outcome more than any hyperparameter. 3DGS needs many sharp, overlapping, consistently exposed views that see every surface you want to render from several directions.

Do:

  • Lock exposure, white balance and focus (an “AE/AF lock” or a manual/pro camera mode). Changing exposure between frames looks like changing materials to the optimizer.
  • Move the camera, not just rotate it. SfM and splatting need parallax: walk around the object or through the room. Pure rotation from one spot gives no depth.
  • Overlap generously: each new photo should share roughly 60–80% of its content with the previous one.
  • For an object: two or three orbits at different heights (e.g. eye level, from above, from low), keeping the object filling a good part of the frame. For a room: walk a loop along the walls facing inwards, and then a second loop facing outwards.
  • Light evenly. Overcast daylight or diffuse indoor lighting is ideal; hard shadows and highlights will be baked in.
  • Typical sizes: 100–300 photos for an object or a small room; several hundred for larger scenes.

Avoid: motion blur (use good light and a fast shutter, or take photos instead of video), moving people and objects, mirrors, glass and very shiny surfaces, large textureless walls, and digital zoom. Ultra-wide and fisheye lenses work but require the right camera model in COLMAP and undistortion.

Video instead of photos. Video is convenient, but each frame has more motion blur and compression. Record at the highest resolution and frame rate available, move slowly, and extract 2–3 frames per second:

mkdir -p scene/input
ffmpeg -i capture.mp4 -qscale:v 1 -qmin 1 -vf "fps=2" scene/input/%04d.jpg

Then delete obviously blurry frames. A quick way to rank them is the variance of the Laplacian (a sharpness score):

import sys, glob
import cv2

paths = sorted(glob.glob(sys.argv[1] + "/*.jpg"))
scores = []
for p in paths:
    g = cv2.imread(p, cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    scores.append((cv2.Laplacian(g, cv2.CV_64F).var(), p))
scores.sort()
print("blurriest 10% (consider deleting):")
for s, p in scores[: max(1, len(scores) // 10)]:
    print(f"{s:8.1f}  {p}")

2. Camera poses with COLMAP

We now run the incremental SfM of post 1. The official 3DGS repository expects this layout:

scene/
  input/          your photos (distorted, any camera model)
  images/         undistorted images            <- created below
  sparse/0/       cameras.bin images.bin points3D.bin (PINHOLE)  <- created below

2.1 The individual steps

cd scene
mkdir -p distorted/sparse

# 1. SIFT features; one shared camera for all images, OPENCV model (k1, k2, p1, p2)
colmap feature_extractor \
    --database_path distorted/database.db \
    --image_path input \
    --ImageReader.single_camera 1 \
    --ImageReader.camera_model OPENCV \
    --FeatureExtraction.use_gpu 1

# 2. Matching: exhaustive for < ~500 images; use sequential_matcher for video frames
colmap exhaustive_matcher \
    --database_path distorted/database.db \
    --FeatureMatching.use_gpu 1

# 3. Incremental SfM (registration, triangulation, bundle adjustment)
colmap mapper \
    --database_path distorted/database.db \
    --image_path input \
    --output_path distorted/sparse

# 4. Undistort to an ideal PINHOLE camera, as required by the 3DGS rasterizer
colmap image_undistorter \
    --image_path input \
    --input_path distorted/sparse/0 \
    --output_path . \
    --output_type COLMAP

# the undistorter writes sparse/*.bin; the 3DGS loader expects sparse/0/
mkdir -p sparse/0 && mv sparse/*.bin sparse/0/

Notes:

  • Option names changed in recent COLMAP releases. Current COLMAP uses --FeatureExtraction.use_gpu and --FeatureMatching.use_gpu; older releases (and the official 3DGS convert.py, which still passes --SiftExtraction.use_gpu / --SiftMatching.use_gpu) use the old names. If convert.py fails at the first step with an unknown-option error, this is why: run the commands above by hand, or edit the two option names in convert.py.
  • single_camera 1 is right when all images come from one camera with fixed zoom; drop it for mixed cameras.
  • With a CPU-only machine, set the use_gpu options to 0. It works, just slower.
  • Global SfM is a faster alternative for large captures. COLMAP now ships a global_mapper command (the GLOMAP approach of post 1); the COLMAP documentation recommends running view_graph_calibrator on a copy of the database first. The standalone GLOMAP reads the same database.

If you prefer the one-liner, the official repository’s script does steps 1–4 for you (put the photos in scene/input first):

python convert.py -s scene            # add --resize to also create 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 images

2.2 Check the reconstruction before training

Five minutes here saves hours later:

colmap model_analyzer --path sparse/0
colmap gui --import_path sparse/0 --database_path distorted/database.db --image_path images

Look for: almost all images registered (if COLMAP split the scene into several models, distorted/sparse/1, 2, … exist and the capture lacks overlap somewhere), a mean reprojection error below about 1 px, and a point cloud and camera trajectory that look like your scene. If cameras are missing, add photos bridging the gap rather than tuning parameters.

3. Training

Pick one of three implementations. They produce compatible .ply files.

3.1 The official INRIA code

git clone https://github.com/graphdeco-inria/gaussian-splatting --recursive
cd gaussian-splatting
conda env create --file environment.yml
conda activate gaussian_splatting

python train.py -s ../scene -m output/scene            # 30k iterations by default
python train.py -s ../scene -m output/scene_eval --eval # hold out every 8th image for testing
python render.py -m output/scene_eval                   # render train/test views
python metrics.py -m output/scene_eval                  # PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS

Useful options of train.py (all from arguments/__init__.py):

Option Effect
-r 2 / -r 4 train at 1/2 or 1/4 resolution (images wider than 1.6K pixels are downscaled automatically)
--data_device cpu keep images in CPU memory if VRAM is short
--iterations 7000 quick preview; the defaults save at 7k and 30k
--densify_grad_threshold 0.0002 the $\tau_{\text{pos}}$ of post 4; raise it to get fewer Gaussians
--antialiasing the 2D Mip filter of Mip-Splatting (post 5) instead of plain dilation
--train_test_exp per-image exposure compensation for captures with exposure changes
--white_background for synthetic scenes with white backgrounds

The trained model is at output/scene/point_cloud/iteration_30000/point_cloud.ply. The repository also contains the SIBR real-time viewer (SIBR_gaussianViewer_app -m output/scene) and a network viewer that can watch training live.

3.2 gsplat

gsplat is faster and lighter in memory, and exposes the variants from post 5 as options.

pip install gsplat
git clone https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/gsplat && cd gsplat/examples
pip install -r requirements.txt --no-build-isolation

# the classic recipe (DefaultStrategy: clone / split / prune)
python simple_trainer.py default --data_dir ../../scene --data_factor 1 \
    --result_dir results/scene --save_ply

# 3DGS-MCMC densification with a fixed Gaussian budget, and anti-aliased rasterization
python simple_trainer.py mcmc --data_dir ../../scene --data_factor 1 \
    --result_dir results/scene_mcmc --antialiased --save_ply

--data_factor 4 reads images downsampled by 4 (it expects an images_4/ folder, which convert.py --resize creates). The .ply files go to results/<name>/ply/point_cloud_<step>.ply, and a browser viewer (Viser) runs during training.

3.3 nerfstudio splatfacto

nerfstudio wraps COLMAP and training in two commands and has the friendliest viewer:

pip install nerfstudio
ns-process-data images --data scene/input --output-dir scene_ns     # or: ns-process-data video --data capture.mp4 ...
ns-train splatfacto --data scene_ns                                  # 'splatfacto-big' for higher quality
ns-export gaussian-splat --load-config outputs/scene_ns/splatfacto/<timestamp>/config.yml \
    --output-dir exports/splat

Splatfacto is built on gsplat. Note that ns-export gaussian-splat only works for splat models, not for NeRF methods such as nerfacto.

3.4 What to expect

Watch the training PSNR and the number of Gaussians. The count grows quickly until densification stops at 15k iterations and then stays flat; one to several million Gaussians is typical for a room or an outdoor scene. A 7k-iteration preview usually tells you whether the capture works. If test-view PSNR is far below training PSNR, the model is overfitting to too few or too similar views: capture more.

4. Inspect, clean and convert the .ply

A 3DGS .ply is a point cloud with extra per-vertex properties: x y z, nx ny nz (unused), f_dc_0..2 (degree-0 SH), f_rest_0..44 (higher SH), opacity (logit), scale_0..2 (log), rot_0..3 (quaternion $w, x, y, z$, unnormalized). The following script prints statistics and removes the most common junk: nearly transparent Gaussians, a few huge blobs and far-away outliers.

import sys
import numpy as np
from plyfile import PlyData, PlyElement

def load_3dgs_ply(path):
    v = PlyData.read(path)["vertex"].data
    xyz = np.stack([v["x"], v["y"], v["z"]], -1)
    opacity = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-v["opacity"]))                      # stored as logits
    scales = np.exp(np.stack([v[f"scale_{i}"] for i in range(3)], -1))   # stored as log-scales
    dc = np.stack([v[f"f_dc_{i}"] for i in range(3)], -1)
    rgb = np.clip(0.5 + 0.28209479177387814 * dc, 0, 1)                 # degree-0 SH -> base colour
    return v, xyz, opacity, scales, rgb

def clean(v, xyz, opacity, scales, min_opacity=0.02, max_scale_pct=99.5, keep_radius_pct=99.0):
    """Drop nearly transparent Gaussians, the largest 'blobs', and far-away outliers."""
    center = np.median(xyz, 0)
    dist = np.linalg.norm(xyz - center, axis=1)
    keep = (opacity > min_opacity)
    keep &= scales.max(1) < np.percentile(scales.max(1), max_scale_pct)
    keep &= dist < np.percentile(dist, keep_radius_pct)
    return v[keep], keep

if __name__ == "__main__":
    src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    v, xyz, opacity, scales, rgb = load_3dgs_ply(src)
    print(f"{len(xyz):,} Gaussians, SH rest coeffs: {sum(n.startswith('f_rest') for n in v.dtype.names)}")
    print("median opacity %.3f, median max-scale %.4f" % (np.median(opacity), np.median(scales.max(1))))
    print("bounding box:", xyz.min(0).round(2), xyz.max(0).round(2))
    kept, mask = clean(v, xyz, opacity, scales)
    print(f"kept {mask.sum():,} / {len(mask):,}")
    PlyData([PlyElement.describe(kept, "vertex")], text=False).write(dst)

pip install plyfile
python clean_ply.py output/scene/point_cloud/iteration_30000/point_cloud.ply scene_clean.ply

Automatic cleaning is a blunt tool; the percentiles are starting points. For precise edits (cropping to a box, deleting floaters by hand, rotating the scene upright) use SuperSplat, PlayCanvas’s open-source browser editor at superspl.at: drag the .ply onto the page, select and delete Gaussians, then export a .ply or a compressed format. Compressed formats are typically several times smaller than the raw .ply, which matters for the web and VR.

5. View it on the web

Several open-source WebGL renderers display 3DGS files; we use Spark, a three.js renderer from World Labs that reads .ply, .spz, .splat, .ksplat and .sog and mixes splats with ordinary three.js meshes. Save this as index.html next to your scene_clean.ply:

<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <style> body { margin: 0; } </style>
  <script type="importmap">
    {
      "imports": {
        "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.180.0/build/three.module.js",
        "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.180.0/examples/jsm/",
        "@sparkjsdev/spark": "https://sparkjs.dev/releases/spark/2.4.0/spark.module.js"
      }
    }
  </script>
</head>
<body>
<script type="module">
  import * as THREE from "three";
  import { OrbitControls } from "three/addons/controls/OrbitControls.js";
  import { VRButton } from "three/addons/webxr/VRButton.js";
  import { SparkRenderer, SplatMesh } from "@sparkjsdev/spark";

  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
  const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(60, innerWidth / innerHeight, 0.01, 1000);
  camera.position.set(0, 1.6, 3);

  const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: false });
  renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
  renderer.xr.enabled = true;                          // WebXR: stereo rendering in a headset
  document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
  document.body.appendChild(VRButton.createButton(renderer));

  scene.add(new SparkRenderer({ renderer }));

  const splat = new SplatMesh({ url: "scene_clean.ply" });
  splat.quaternion.set(1, 0, 0, 0);                    // COLMAP is y-down: rotate 180 deg about x
  splat.position.set(0, 1.2, 0);                       // put the scene around eye height
  scene.add(splat);

  const controls = new OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement);
  controls.target.set(0, 1.2, 0);
  addEventListener("resize", () => {
    camera.aspect = innerWidth / innerHeight;
    camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
    renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
  });
  renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
    controls.update();
    renderer.render(scene, camera);
  });
</script>
</body>
</html>

Serve the folder over HTTP (browsers block module loading from file://):

python -m http.server 8000      # then open http://localhost:8000

The rotation line matters: COLMAP and 3DGS use the OpenCV convention with $y$ pointing down (post 1), while three.js uses $y$ up. The quaternion $(x, y, z, w) = (1, 0, 0, 0)$ in three.js’s order is a 180° rotation about the $x$ axis. If your scene is still tilted, it is because COLMAP’s world frame is arbitrary (post 1, gauge freedom): straighten it once in SuperSplat, or estimate the up direction as the average of the cameras’ up vectors.

Other viewers worth knowing: the PlayCanvas engine and SuperSplat’s own publishing (which creates a shareable viewer page), GaussianSplats3D for three.js, the original WebGL viewer antimatter15/splat, and the official SIBR viewer on the desktop.

6. View it in VR

The page above is already VR-ready: renderer.xr.enabled plus the Enter VR button from VRButton start a WebXR session, and three.js renders the scene once per eye with the headset’s tracked pose. To use it on a standalone headset:

  1. Serve over HTTPS or use port forwarding. WebXR requires a secure context. localhost counts as secure, so the easiest route is to connect the headset by USB and forward the port (for example adb reverse tcp:8000 tcp:8000 for Android-based headsets), then open http://localhost:8000 in the headset browser. Alternatively host the folder on any HTTPS static host (GitHub Pages works).
  2. Mind the scale and origin. SfM units are arbitrary (post 1). If the room looks like a doll house or a cathedral, scale the SplatMesh uniformly (splat.scale.setScalar(k)) using a known distance, and position it so the floor is at $y = 0$ for a local-floor reference space.
  3. Respect the budget. A standalone headset renders two views at 72–90 Hz on a mobile GPU. Spark’s documentation suggests budgets of roughly half a million to three quarters of a million splats for WebXR, compared with millions on desktop. Reduce the count by training with a budget (gsplat mcmc, e.g. via its --strategy.cap_max option), raising the densification threshold, or decimating in SuperSplat, and prefer compressed files.
  4. Reduce popping and aliasing. Head motion exposes sorting pops and aliasing. Train with --antialiasing (official code) or --antialiased (gsplat) if you will view the scene at different distances from the capture.

Spark also includes its own WebXR helper (SparkXr) with controller and hand-tracking locomotion, and SuperSplat’s published viewer supports WebXR in AR and VR. For native engines, community plugins bring Gaussian splats to Unity and Unreal; check that they support single-pass stereo before you rely on them for VR.

7. Common failure modes

Symptom Likely cause Fix
COLMAP registers only part of the images, or several models gaps in overlap, repetitive or textureless areas add bridging photos; use sequential_matcher for video; try global_mapper; mask out sky or moving objects
convert.py fails at feature extraction renamed COLMAP options (SiftExtraction.* → FeatureExtraction.*) run the commands of section 2.1, or edit convert.py
Training crashes with out-of-memory too many pixels or Gaussians -r 2, --data_device cpu, raise --densify_grad_threshold, or use gsplat with a Gaussian cap
Floaters near the cameras unconstrained space in front of the cameras, few views per region more views; rely on opacity reset; remove in SuperSplat; depth regularization if available
Blurry everywhere motion blur, wrong focus, bad poses delete blurry frames; check the reprojection error; lock focus
Colour flicker or “patchy” exposure auto exposure or white balance changed lock exposure; --train_test_exp (official) or appearance embeddings (splatfacto)
Needle-like spikes or shimmer when zooming in or out aliasing (post 5) --antialiasing / --antialiased; avoid rendering far outside the capture distance
Good from capture positions, broken in between views too similar (no parallax) or SH “painting” move the camera more; capture more varied viewpoints
Mirrors and windows look like holes or second rooms view-dependent effects 3DGS cannot explain expected; mask or avoid such surfaces; reflections are an open research problem
Scene tilted or upside down in the viewer arbitrary SfM frame, y-down convention rotate 180° about $x$; straighten in SuperSplat
Wrong scale in VR SfM scale is arbitrary scale by a measured reference distance

8. Where to go from here

  • Evaluate properly. Use --eval and report PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS on held-out views (post 2), not on training views.
  • Try the variants of post 5. 2DGS for meshes (gsplat ships simple_trainer_2dgs.py), MCMC densification, compression for the web.
  • Make it interactive. Combine the splat with three.js meshes for UI and physics, or segment it and let users manipulate objects, as in VR-GS.
  • Feed-forward instead of optimization. For sparse or unposed photos, try the feed-forward models of post 5 and compare with your optimized result.

Try it

Before your first capture, open the Gaussian World demo in the interactive lab and switch to the “Ellipsoids” and “Overdraw” views: they show what a well-distributed set of Gaussians looks like, and how much overdraw a VR frame has to pay for, the same quantities you will be tuning in sections 3 and 6.

Representative papers and tools

Paper / tool Venue Year Link Why it matters
Structure-from-Motion Revisited (COLMAP, Schönberger & Frahm) CVPR 2016 CVF The pose estimation step of this tutorial
Global Structure-from-Motion Revisited (GLOMAP, Pan et al.) ECCV 2024 arXiv Fast global SfM for large captures
3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering (Kerbl et al.) ACM TOG / SIGGRAPH 2023 arXiv The method we train
Nerfstudio (Tancik et al.) SIGGRAPH (Conf.) 2023 arXiv Processing, splatfacto and viewer
gsplat: An Open-Source Library for Gaussian Splatting (Ye et al.) arXiv 2024 arXiv Fast trainer with MCMC and anti-aliasing
Mip-Splatting (Yu et al.) CVPR 2024 arXiv Why --antialiasing matters in VR
3D Gaussian Splatting as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Kheradmand et al.) NeurIPS 2024 arXiv Budgeted densification for VR-sized models
VR-GS (Jiang et al.) SIGGRAPH 2024 arXiv A full interactive Gaussian VR system

Learning resources

  • COLMAP documentation: tutorial, command-line interface, FAQ (including tips for difficult datasets).
  • Official 3DGS repository: README sections on processing your own scenes and the viewers.
  • gsplat documentation and its examples/ folder.
  • nerfstudio documentation, including the data capture guides and splatfacto.
  • Spark and its examples; SuperSplat; the WebXR Device API and three.js WebXR examples.

Exercises

  1. Capture the same object twice: once with auto exposure and once with exposure locked. Train both and compare test PSNR and visual artefacts.
  2. Train with -r 4 and at full resolution, then view both at full resolution in the browser, with and without --antialiasing. Describe the differences in terms of post 5.
  3. Use clean_ply.py and SuperSplat to reduce your model to under 500k Gaussians; measure the frame rate in the headset before and after.
  4. Write a small script that reads images.bin (e.g. with pycolmap) and estimates the scene’s up vector from the cameras; use it to straighten the model automatically in the web viewer.
  5. Measure a known distance in your scene (a table length) and set the VR scale so that it is correct; check it in the headset with your hands.

This is the last post of the neural rendering track. The world-models and embodied-AI series build on it: Gaussian maps for robots, generated Gaussian worlds, and simulators that render what a camera would see.
entry.summary: A practical, step-by-step workflow: capture photos or video, run COLMAP, train 3DGS with the official code, gsplat or nerfstudio splatfacto, clean and export the .ply, and view it on the web and in a VR headset, with common failure modes and fixes.

entry.title: Beyond 3DGS: a map of the Gaussian splatting frontier

link.title: Beyond 3DGS: a map of the Gaussian splatting frontier

entry.content:
Why this matters

Post 4 covered the original 3DGS method. Within a year of its publication there were hundreds of follow-ups, and by now Gaussians are used far beyond novel view synthesis: as maps for robots, as outputs of feed-forward and generative models, as simulation particles, and as the content format for web and VR viewers. This post is a map, not an exhaustive list. For each direction it explains what limitation of vanilla 3DGS is addressed, the key technical idea (often a single equation), and two or three representative papers to read first. Use the reading list at the end of the series for more.

A useful way to organize the field is by which part of the 3DGS pipeline a paper changes:

Pipeline stage What gets changed Directions in this post
Primitive shape, dimensionality, attributes surfaces (2D/flat Gaussians), dynamics (4D), semantics, relighting
Projection and rasterization filtering, sorting, ray tracing anti-aliasing, popping, ray-traced Gaussians
Optimization densification, regularizers, losses MCMC densification, surface regularizers, compression
Where parameters come from per-scene optimization vs networks SLAM, feed-forward reconstruction, generation
What happens after simulation, editing, display physics, AR/VR

Prerequisites

  • The full 3DGS method: covariance, EWA projection, blending, density control (post 4).
  • NeRF follow-ups (Mip-NeRF, NeRF-W; post 2), and K-Planes (post 3).
  • For SLAM and feed-forward models: camera poses (post 1) and basic transformers/diffusion models.

1. Anti-aliasing: Mip-Splatting

Problem. 3DGS adds a fixed $0.3\,I$ dilation in screen space (post 4, section 2.1). Train at one resolution and render at a much higher one (zoom in), and Gaussians that were sub-pixel during training become thin, high-frequency artefacts; render at a lower resolution (zoom out) and the dilation makes everything look too thick and bright, because it adds energy without normalization.

Key idea. Mip-Splatting (Yu, Chen, Huang, Sattler & Geiger, CVPR 2024) uses two filters:

  • A 3D smoothing filter limits the frequency of each Gaussian based on the maximal sampling rate of the training views. For Gaussian $k$, $\hat\nu_k = \max_n f_n / d_{k,n}$ over training cameras $n$ that see it (focal length in pixels over depth). The Gaussian is convolved with an isotropic Gaussian of variance $s/\hat\nu_k^2$, and the opacity is rescaled so the integral is preserved:
\[\Sigma_k \leftarrow \Sigma_k + \frac{s}{\hat\nu_k^{2}}\, I, \qquad o_k \leftarrow o_k \sqrt{\frac{\lvert \Sigma_k \rvert}{\lvert \Sigma_k + \frac{s}{\hat\nu_k^{2}} I \rvert}} .\]

The filter becomes part of the Gaussian, so it is applied consistently from every viewpoint, and it prevents Gaussians from becoming thinner than the data can justify.

  • A 2D Mip filter replaces the dilation with a normalized Gaussian approximating a one-pixel box filter, $\Sigma’_{2D} = \Sigma’ + sI$ with $o$ scaled by $\sqrt{\lvert\Sigma’\rvert / \lvert \Sigma’ + sI\rvert}$, which simulates the integration over a pixel area when zooming out.
import numpy as np

def max_sampling_rate(means, cams):
    """nu_k = max over training cameras that see Gaussian k of focal / depth (pixels per world unit)."""
    nu = np.zeros(len(means))
    for R, t, f, W, H in cams:
        Xc = means @ R.T + t
        z = Xc[:, 2]
        u, v = f * Xc[:, 0] / np.maximum(z, 1e-6) + W / 2, f * Xc[:, 1] / np.maximum(z, 1e-6) + H / 2
        visible = (z > 0.2) & (u >= 0) & (u < W) & (v >= 0) & (v < H)
        nu = np.where(visible, np.maximum(nu, f / np.maximum(z, 1e-6)), nu)
    return nu

def smooth_3d(Sigma, opacity, nu, s=0.2):
    """Mip-Splatting 3D smoothing: convolve each Gaussian with an isotropic Gaussian of
    variance s / nu^2 and rescale opacity so that the integral stays the same."""
    add = (s / np.maximum(nu, 1e-6) ** 2)[:, None, None] * np.eye(3)
    Sigma_f = Sigma + add
    scale = np.sqrt(np.linalg.det(Sigma) / np.linalg.det(Sigma_f))
    return Sigma_f, opacity * scale

def mip_filter_2d(cov2d, opacity, s=0.1):
    """Replace 3DGS's '+0.3 I' dilation by a normalized 2D filter approximating a 1-pixel box."""
    cov_f = cov2d + s * np.eye(2)
    return cov_f, opacity * np.sqrt(np.linalg.det(cov2d) / np.linalg.det(cov_f))

Mip-Splatting is the 3DGS counterpart of Mip-NeRF’s integrated positional encoding: in both cases a point sample is replaced by a footprint-aware, low-passed one. It is cheap and implemented as an option in gsplat; consider enabling it whenever renders will be viewed at resolutions different from the capture, which is the norm in VR.

2. Surfaces and geometry

Problem. 3DGS optimizes appearance, not geometry. Its Gaussians are volumetric blobs whose depth along a ray is ill-defined, normals do not exist, and extracting a mesh with marching cubes on the opacity yields noisy, bumpy surfaces. Robotics, physics and editing all need surfaces.

Key ideas.

  • SuGaR (Guédon & Lepetit, CVPR 2024) adds a regularizer that drives Gaussians to be flat and well distributed on the surface, so that the density can be approximated by an SDF-like function near the surface. A mesh is then extracted with Poisson reconstruction from level-set samples, and new Gaussians are bound to the mesh triangles for joint refinement, giving an editable, animatable hybrid.
  • 2D Gaussian Splatting (Huang, Yu, Chen, Geiger & Gao, SIGGRAPH 2024) collapses each primitive to an oriented planar disk (a surfel) with two tangent vectors $\mathbf t_u, \mathbf t_v$ and two scales $s_u, s_v$. A point on the disk is $P(u,v) = \mathbf p_k + s_u \mathbf t_u u + s_v \mathbf t_v v$, the normal is $\mathbf t_u \times \mathbf t_v$, and instead of EWA linearization each pixel’s ray is intersected exactly with the disk’s plane, giving perspective-correct, view-consistent depth. Two regularizers make it geometry-aware: a depth-distortion loss (from Mip-NeRF 360) that concentrates weights along each ray, and a normal-consistency loss that aligns the splat normals with normals computed from the rendered depth map. Meshes are extracted by TSDF fusion of rendered depth.
  • Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) (Yu, Sattler & Geiger, ACM TOG / SIGGRAPH Asia 2024) define a continuous opacity field directly from 3D Gaussians via ray–Gaussian intersection, and extract the surface as a level set with marching tetrahedra on a grid induced by the Gaussians, which handles unbounded scenes and adapts resolution to detail.

The general lesson: if you need geometry, choose a primitive whose depth and normal are well defined (flat Gaussians or disks) and add geometric regularization. 2DGS-style surfels have become a common choice in mapping and robotics pipelines.

3. Dynamic scenes

Problem. 3DGS assumes a static scene. For moving people, objects or deformable scenes we need the Gaussians to change over time while staying consistent, from multi-view video or even a single monocular video.

Four designs dominate:

  1. Per-frame tracking. Dynamic 3D Gaussians (Luiten, Kopanas, Leibe & Ramanan, 3DV 2024) keep colour, opacity and size fixed and optimize each Gaussian’s position and rotation per time step, with local rigidity regularizers between neighbours. Dense 6-DoF tracking of every scene element emerges as a by-product, with no correspondence or flow supervision.
  2. Canonical space + deformation network. Deformable 3D Gaussians (Yang et al., CVPR 2024) learn Gaussians in a canonical space and an MLP $\mathcal F_\theta(\gamma(\mathbf x), \gamma(t)) \mapsto (\delta\mathbf x, \delta\mathbf r, \delta\mathbf s)$ that deforms them at time $t$, trained on monocular video.
  3. Canonical space + factorized field. 4D Gaussian Splatting (Wu et al., CVPR 2024) replaces the MLP by a HexPlane-style decomposition (six feature planes over $xy, xz, yz, xt, yt, zt$, as in K-Planes of post 3) followed by a tiny decoder, which is faster and more compact; the paper reports real-time rendering (82 fps at $800\times800$ on synthetic data).
  4. Native 4D primitives. In “Real-time Photorealistic Dynamic Scene Representation and Rendering with 4D Gaussian Splatting” (Yang et al., ICLR 2024), each primitive is a Gaussian in $(x, y, z, t)$. Rendering at time $t$ conditions it on $t$, which yields a 3D Gaussian whose mean moves linearly in time and whose opacity is modulated by the temporal marginal:
\[\boldsymbol\mu_{xyz\mid t} = \boldsymbol\mu_{1:3} + \Sigma_{1:3,4}\,\Sigma_{4,4}^{-1}(t - \mu_4), \qquad \Sigma_{xyz\mid t} = \Sigma_{1:3,1:3} - \Sigma_{1:3,4}\,\Sigma_{4,4}^{-1}\,\Sigma_{4,1:3}, \qquad p(t) \propto \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{(t-\mu_4)^2}{2\Sigma_{4,4}}\Big).\] 
def slice_4d(mu4, Sigma4, t):
    """Condition a 4D (x, y, z, t) Gaussian on time t: returns the 3D mean, 3D covariance and the
    temporal marginal p(t) (unnormalized), as in native 4D Gaussian splatting."""
    S11, S12, S22 = Sigma4[:3, :3], Sigma4[:3, 3], Sigma4[3, 3]
    mu3 = mu4[:3] + S12 / S22 * (t - mu4[3])
    Sigma3 = S11 - np.outer(S12, S12) / S22
    p_t = np.exp(-0.5 * (t - mu4[3]) ** 2 / S22)
    return mu3, Sigma3, p_t

Related designs include Spacetime Gaussians (Li et al., CVPR 2024), with polynomial motion and rotation, temporal radial-basis opacity, and neural features instead of SH, and articulated or rigged models such as GaussianAvatars (Qian et al., CVPR 2024), which attach Gaussians to the triangles of a parametric face model so that expressions and head pose drive them directly. Monocular dynamic reconstruction remains hard: a single moving camera does not constrain fast non-rigid motion, so the best systems add priors such as depth, optical flow, or point tracks from foundation models.

4. Compression and efficiency

Problem. A 3DGS scene often takes hundreds of megabytes to more than a gigabyte, mostly in the 48 SH coefficients, and contains many redundant Gaussians. That is too much for streaming, mobile and VR.

The toolbox, roughly in order of how aggressive it is:

  • Pruning by importance. Score each Gaussian by how much it contributes to the training views (e.g. accumulated $\alpha_i T_i$ over all pixels) and remove the least useful. LightGaussian (Fan et al., NeurIPS 2024) combines such pruning with SH distillation to lower degrees and vector quantization, and reports an average compression of about 15× with a higher frame rate.
  • Learned masks and codebooks. Compact 3D Gaussian Representation (Lee et al., CVPR 2024) learns a mask that removes Gaussians during training, stores view-dependent colour in a hash grid instead of per-Gaussian SH, and vector-quantizes geometry attributes.
  • Structured anchors. Scaffold-GS (Lu et al., CVPR 2024) stores sparse anchor points with features and decodes local Gaussians on the fly with small MLPs conditioned on view direction and distance. It is more compact and more robust to view-dependent effects.
  • Entropy coding. HAC (Chen et al., ECCV 2024) builds on Scaffold-GS and uses a binarized hash grid as context to model the distribution of anchor attributes for entropy coding, reporting more than 75× size reduction over vanilla 3DGS.

Practical formats have followed: viewers such as SuperSplat and Spark read compressed formats (e.g. SPZ and SOG) alongside the original .ply. For speed, the main tricks are fewer Gaussians (MCMC-style budgets, pruning), lower SH degrees, and better load balancing in the rasterizer.

5. Rendering quality and correctness

A few papers fix limitations of the renderer itself:

  • Popping. Sorting by Gaussian centre per tile changes order abruptly under rotation. StopThePop (Radl et al., ACM TOG / SIGGRAPH 2024) approximates per-pixel sorting with a hierarchical rasterizer at about 4% extra cost on average, and finds that enforcing consistency lets it halve the number of Gaussians. This matters most in VR, where head rotation is constant.
  • Ray tracing. 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (Moenne-Loccoz et al., SIGGRAPH Asia 2024) encloses Gaussians in bounding primitives inside a BVH and traces rays with hardware ray tracing, enabling distorted cameras (fisheye, rolling shutter), secondary rays for reflections and shadows, and exact per-ray ordering, at some speed cost.
  • Densification. 3DGS as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Kheradmand et al., NeurIPS 2024) interprets the Gaussians as samples and the updates as stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, replacing clone/split heuristics with relocation of dead Gaussians and a fixed budget, which is more robust to initialization.

6. SLAM: Gaussians as maps

Problem. A robot or headset needs to localize and map online, with unknown poses, from a stream of frames. Classic dense SLAM uses TSDF volumes, surfels or neural fields; Gaussians offer photorealistic, differentiable maps that can be rendered from any pose in milliseconds.

Key idea. Alternate tracking, optimizing the current camera pose by minimizing photometric (and depth) error between the incoming frame and the rendering of the map with the map frozen, and mapping, optimizing the Gaussians on keyframes with the poses frozen, while adding new Gaussians where the map is incomplete. Differentiable rasterization makes both steps gradient-based.

  • SplaTAM (Keetha et al., CVPR 2024) targets RGB-D input. It renders a silhouette (accumulated opacity) to know which pixels the current map explains, uses only those for tracking, and densifies where the silhouette is low or new geometry appears in front of the map. It uses simplified isotropic, view-independent Gaussians.
  • Gaussian Splatting SLAM / MonoGS (Matsuki, Murai, Kelly & Davison, CVPR 2024) is the first to work with a monocular camera (and extends to RGB-D). It derives analytic Jacobians of the rendering with respect to the camera pose on the Lie group $SE(3)$, regularizes Gaussians to stay isotropic for stable incremental mapping, and manages a keyframe window.

For embodied AI this is a key bridge: a Gaussian map is simultaneously a localization map, a photorealistic simulator for the robot’s camera, and, with semantic features (section 10), a queryable scene representation.

7. Feed-forward reconstruction

Problem. Per-scene optimization takes minutes and needs many posed views. Can a network predict Gaussians from a few images in a single forward pass?

Key idea. Predict pixel-aligned Gaussians: for each pixel of each input view, the network outputs a depth along the pixel’s ray (hence a 3D mean), a covariance, an opacity and a colour. Training uses large multi-view datasets with the same rendering loss as 3DGS, on held-out target views.

  • pixelSplat (Charatan, Li, Tagliasacchi & Sitzmann, CVPR 2024) reconstructs a scene from an image pair. An epipolar transformer resolves scale, and instead of regressing depth directly, the network predicts a probability distribution over depth buckets and samples the Gaussian mean from it, using a reparameterization trick so gradients flow to the probabilities.
  • MVSplat (Chen et al., ECCV 2024) builds a plane-sweep cost volume (the multi-view stereo of post 1, learned) to localize Gaussian centres, which is more geometric and reported to use 10× fewer parameters than pixelSplat while running more than 2× faster.
  • The large reconstruction model line scales this up with transformers. LRM (Hong et al., ICLR 2024) predicts a triplane NeRF from a single image with a 500M-parameter transformer trained on about a million objects; GS-LRM (Zhang et al., ECCV 2024) patchifies posed images, runs a transformer over all tokens and decodes per-pixel Gaussians; LGM (Tang et al., ECCV 2024) maps four views (generated by a multi-view diffusion model) to Gaussians with an asymmetric U-Net within seconds.

Pose-free variants combine these ideas with DUSt3R/MASt3R/VGGT-style geometry networks (post 1), so that unposed photos go straight to splats. Feed-forward reconstruction is also how 3D world generation is increasingly built: a generator produces images or video, and a reconstruction network lifts them to Gaussians.

8. Generation: text and images to Gaussians

Problem. Create 3D content without captured data.

Key idea 1: score distillation. DreamFusion (post 2) optimizes a 3D representation $\theta$ so that its renderings $\mathbf x = g(\theta)$ look plausible to a frozen text-to-image diffusion model $\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_\phi$, via the score distillation sampling (SDS) gradient

\[\nabla_\theta \mathcal L_{\text{SDS}} = \mathbb E_{t, \boldsymbol\epsilon}\Big[ w(t)\,\big(\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}_\phi(\mathbf x_t; y, t) - \boldsymbol\epsilon\big)\, \frac{\partial \mathbf x}{\partial \theta} \Big],\]

where $\mathbf x_t$ is the noised rendering at noise level $t$ and $y$ the prompt. Gaussians are a far faster $\theta$ than NeRFs: DreamGaussian (Tang et al., ICLR 2024) runs SDS on Gaussians with progressive densification, then extracts a textured mesh and refines its UV texture, producing assets in minutes. GaussianDreamer (Yi et al., CVPR 2024) initializes the Gaussians from a 3D diffusion model’s coarse output and refines them with 2D diffusion, combining 3D consistency with 2D detail.

Key idea 2: generate views, then reconstruct. Multi-view diffusion models generate a consistent set of views, and a feed-forward model (LGM, GS-LRM, section 7) turns them into Gaussians. This is faster and avoids SDS’s oversaturation, and it extends to scenes: video or panorama generators followed by reconstruction produce explorable Gaussian worlds, the idea behind products such as World Labs’ Marble, which the Gaussian World demo on the home page imitates procedurally.

9. Relighting and inverse rendering

Problem. 3DGS bakes the capture’s lighting into SH colour, so a captured object cannot be placed under new lighting, which is exactly what AR and content creation need.

Key idea. Give each Gaussian physically based attributes (a normal, albedo, roughness, metallic) and model lighting explicitly (an environment map plus visibility), then render with a differentiable shading model, essentially the BRDF machinery of the PBR post, evaluated per Gaussian or per pixel in a deferred pass. The hard parts are normals (Gaussians have none, so they are derived from the shortest axis or from rendered depth) and visibility.

  • Relightable 3D Gaussians (Gao et al., ECCV 2024) attach normals, BRDF parameters and incident lighting to each Gaussian, decompose them with physically based differentiable rendering, and compute visibility by point-based ray tracing on a BVH over Gaussians, enabling relighting with shadows.
  • GS-IR (Liang et al., CVPR 2024) regularizes normals with rendered depth and bakes occlusion into a volume to approximate indirect illumination, recovering geometry, materials and lighting under unknown illumination.

The Gaussian World demo takes the opposite route: its Gaussians are generated with albedo and normals rather than inverted from photos, so it can relight them for any time of day by construction.

10. Physics, semantics and editing

Physics. Gaussians are particles, so they can be simulated. PhysGaussian (Xie et al., CVPR 2024) treats each Gaussian as a particle of a Material Point Method (MPM) continuum simulation. When the material deforms with local deformation gradient $\mathbf F$, the covariance deforms accordingly,

\[\Sigma_t = \mathbf F_t\, \Sigma_0\, \mathbf F_t^\top ,\]

and the SH coefficients are rotated by the rotational part of $\mathbf F_t$, so that “what you see is what you simulate” without converting to meshes. VR-GS (Jiang et al., SIGGRAPH 2024) builds an interactive VR system that embeds Gaussians in tetrahedral cages simulated with XPBD (extended position-based dynamics) for real-time manipulation, with segmentation, inpainting and shadows. The XPBD cloth demo in the interactive lab uses the same solver family.

Semantics. Attaching features to Gaussians makes scenes queryable. LangSplat (Qin et al., CVPR 2024) distills CLIP language features, organized by SAM’s hierarchy of masks, into per-Gaussian latent features through a scene-specific autoencoder, enabling open-vocabulary 3D queries (“where is the mug?”) much faster than NeRF-based language fields. This is the representation that robots can use to ground instructions in a 3D map.

Editing. Because Gaussians are explicit, selection, deletion, transformation and compositing are straightforward, which tools such as SuperSplat expose interactively. Diffusion-guided editing methods modify appearance or geometry with text instructions.

11. AR and VR

Why Gaussians suit XR. They render photoreal captures at high frame rates with a simple rasterizer, run in browsers and on standalone headsets, and require no meshing or texture baking.

What makes XR hard.

  • Frame budget. Stereo rendering at 72–120 Hz per eye on mobile GPUs leaves a few milliseconds for millions of Gaussians, on top of sorting. Compression and Gaussian budgets (section 4) and level-of-detail streaming are therefore essential; web renderers such as Spark (World Labs) now stream large splat scenes with level of detail across desktop, mobile and VR.
  • Artefacts are more visible. Popping (section 5) under constant head motion, aliasing when the viewer moves closer than the capture (section 1), and inconsistent depth between the two eyes all break immersion. Mip filtering and consistent sorting help.
  • Foveated rendering. Rendering fewer or larger Gaussians in the periphery exploits the falloff of visual acuity; see the foveated rendering demo in the lab for the underlying idea.
  • Interaction and relighting. Placing virtual objects into a captured room needs consistent lighting (section 9), occlusion from accurate depth (section 2) and physics (section 10); VR-GS is a good example of putting these together.

For research at the intersection with HCI, open questions include perceptual quality metrics for splats in VR, interaction techniques for selecting and editing millions of soft primitives, and capture interfaces that guide users to collect good coverage (post 6).

Try it

The interactive lab connects to several sections: Gaussian World (rendering, and generation by a procedural stand-in, section 8; relightable Gaussians, section 9), XPBD cloth (the physics family used by VR-GS, section 10) and foveated rendering (section 11).

Representative papers

Learning resources

  • The official code of most papers above is linked from their arXiv pages; gsplat implements several of them (Mip-Splatting filters, MCMC densification, 2DGS rasterization) behind one API.
  • The radiancefields.com news site tracks new Gaussian splatting papers, tools and products.
  • The reading list docs/reading-lists/neural-rendering.md in the repository of this website groups the papers by stage.
  • For the graphics background of sections 9–10, the PBR and simulation posts of the graphics series.

Exercises

  1. Show that convolving a Gaussian of covariance $\Sigma$ (peak 1, opacity $o$) with a normalized isotropic Gaussian of variance $v$ gives a Gaussian of covariance $\Sigma + vI$ and peak $o\sqrt{\lvert\Sigma\rvert/\lvert\Sigma+vI\rvert}$. This is the opacity rescaling of Mip-Splatting.
  2. Verify slice_4d numerically: sample from a random 4D Gaussian, keep the samples with $\lvert t - t_0\rvert < \varepsilon$, and compare their mean and covariance with the formula.
  3. In the PyTorch renderer of post 4, replace the + 0.3 * I dilation by mip_filter_2d and compare renders at $0.5\times$ and $4\times$ the training resolution.
  4. Sketch a SplaTAM-style tracking step with the renderer of post 4: freeze the Gaussians, make the camera rotation (axis-angle) and translation learnable, and minimize L1 to a target image rendered from a perturbed pose.
  5. Pick one direction and read its two representative papers. Write a half-page summary of what problem each solves, its key equation, and one failure case.

Next: post 6 is hands-on: capture your own scene, run COLMAP, train a splat, and look at it on the web and in VR.
entry.summary: A structured survey of what came after 3D Gaussian Splatting: anti-aliasing, surfaces, dynamic scenes, compression, SLAM, feed-forward reconstruction, generation, relighting, physics, semantics and AR/VR, with the key idea and representative papers of each direction.

entry.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting, end to end
